questions.question_text: Two cakes are different sizes. Each has $\tfrac{1}{2}$ left. What can be concluded?

options.text: The larger cake has more cake left.

options.why: This assumes equal wholes even though the cakes are different sizes.

options.text: The smaller cake has more left.
options.why: This reverses the effect of taking the same fraction of different wholes.

questions.solution_text:
The same fraction is taken from each cake.
The larger whole gives the larger remaining amount.

questions.question_text: Two equal pizzas are shared. Lee eats $\tfrac{3}{8}$ and Jo eats $\tfrac{5}{8}$. Who eats more?

options.why: This treats the smaller numerator as the larger share.
This ignores that the numerators are different for equal wholes.

questions.question_text: Half of a $14$ m rope is compared with half of a $10$ m rope. What is the difference?

options.why: This assumes equal fractions give equal amounts for unequal wholes.
This subtracts the rope lengths without first taking halves.
This adds the two half-lengths instead of finding their difference.

questions.question_text: Can $\tfrac{2}{5}$ of one mystery tank be fairly compared with $\tfrac{4}{5}$ of another?

options.text: No, not without the container capacities.

options.why: This compares numerators while ignoring that the wholes may differ.
Matching denominators do not make different wholes the same size.

questions.solution_text:
The fractions refer to different unknown wholes.
No fair amount comparison can be made.

questions.question_text: Tank A: $\tfrac{3}{4}$ of $32$ L. Tank B: $\tfrac{5}{6}$ of $30$ L. Which contains more?

options.why: This reverses the two calculated quantities.
This compares only the unused parts of the tanks.
This rounds the two different quantities to the same value.

questions.solution_text:
Tank A: $32\div4\times3=24$ L
Tank B: $30\div6\times5=25$ L
$25-24=1$ L

questions.question_text: A student adds $\tfrac{1}{4}$ of a bucket and $\tfrac{2}{4}$ of a cup to get $\tfrac{3}{4}$ of a bucket. Which check was missed?

options.text: Check that both fractions refer to the same whole.
Check that both numerators are odd.
options.why: Numerator parity does not determine whether fractions can be combined.

options.text: Check that both denominators are different.
options.why: The denominators already match; the whole-size mismatch is the issue.

questions.solution_text:
The bucket and cup are different wholes.
Their fractional amounts cannot be combined as parts of one bucket.
